touches.text: Two callers waking the same part at once start only one: the part that binds its socket first is the only one; a second copy finds it taken and exits quietly (as the ground loop does, 5.6.4.3).

The second copy exits SILENTLY; refusing loudly has no reason behind it. A --force switch means "don't exit if another is running: kill the other and take over", for replacing a running older version with a newer one. Akien 2026-11-13, answering Q#93 (ticket b38af5fd1852 says loud, this line says quiet), about the ground loop: "why? if i try and run ground loop and it's already running it should exit silently. otoh, that means we should have a switch like --force that means don't exit if another is running, --force means force it, kill the other process. useful when you're specically replacing a running older version with a newer one." CC's read, not yet his word: the same holds for every host singleton (bus, rack, a device name).

Akien 2026-11-13, said in akiendell's session, answering the same Q#93 on a second asking (verbatim): "no there's no conflict there. those are completely different kinds of things. spinning up a second ground loop should see the first, and that it's fine, and exit quietly. if we're starting a new one on purpose, like there's an older one running, we'll add --force, which means kill the old one. we change that intention. i have no recollection why it says loudly. but the naming, yes. if we had two zeros how would messages get routed? or <host>_cc_RESCUE? we DO want to be able to spin up more than one of something. many things can be singletons or not... like the embeddings generator. if we wound up with too much traffic, we might open a second on another host. but the launcher has to ask the shim to create the instance, and so it's the shim's job to say 'we've been asked to start and instance, then we've not been given a name for it, then we have a cc_0 instance, so I'll launch it with cc_1'"

One bus per cairn instance, not per host. Each box runs its own bus, and the buses talk to one another, so a device always talks to the bus on its own box; together they are the instance's one bus. A device runs on one box; the other boxes reach it over the buses. No box needs a full set of devices. WHY: so the instance can run several heavy tasks at once across boxes.

Every box runs all the foundational things: a bus, a ground loop, the shims. They are the Cairn device's machines, and there is only one Cairn device: a singleton within the swarm, owning them on every box. WHY: Cairn is the system in aggregate, which is not the same thing as the host (6.6); a box is part of the host, and the swarm of boxes is still one Cairn.
A second copy refuses to start.
